In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?
Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.
It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.
Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.
Here are some key points:
- The nominal Fed funds rate was substantially higher in 1995 than it is today. The real, or inflation adjusted, funds rate was a positive 3.75% back then, and it's now at zero. So the Fed was leaning against the dotcom boom. Greenspan just decided not to lean more. Today, at a zero real rate, the Fed could be said to be fueling the boom.
- Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, was substantially lower, right about target at 1.99% (even though there wasn't a formal 2% target then). It's above target now, at 3.8% according to government data published today, and going the wrong way.
- The current investment boom now is absolutely off the charts compared with the dot-com era. No real comparison. In 1995, spending on information processing equipment rose 15% year over year. In 2025, it was 27%. Looking at the latest data reported today, it grew 60% in the third quarter at an annualized rate. In the second quarter of 1995, it was 18%.
- Government deficit spending is substantially more stimulative now than it was then. In 1995, the deficit was just 2.2% of GDP. Today, it's 6.2%.
- Add higher oil prices, higher tariffs and the recent tax cuts and accelerated depreciation on investments, and there's a lot for the Fed to lean against.
It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. Baseball was a joy to watch in 2026 – as it always is. We saw seasoned veteran stars continue to awe and new names join those ranks of the best in the game. We said goodbye to fan favorites and witnessed historic firsts. We spent time on the edge of our seats, locked in on the drama. In short, baseball was the best, yet again.
It can’t possibly all be covered in one story, so we’ll also have the MLB milestones reached in 2026 coming later this week.
Here are 26 things we’re thankful for from the 2026 season.
For Ueck
They finally did it. After beginning in 1969 as the Seattle Pilots, the Brewers franchise played 57 seasons before their first title-winning campaign. That’s the fourth-longest drought before winning a franchise’s first World Series. The Phillies played 77 seasons between the first Fall Classic in 1903 and their first title-winning season in 1980, 63 for the Orioles/Browns and 62 for the Rangers/Senators.
The Brewers went 11-2 this postseason. They’re the fifth team to win at least 11 games and lose two or fewer in a postseason, joining the 2022 Astros (11-2), 2005 White Sox (11-1), 1999 Yankees (11-1) and 1998 Yankees (11-2).
Milwaukee arms
The pitching was a key component of that dominance. The Brewers did not allow more than four runs in any of their 13 postseason games. They joined the 1990 Reds and 1983 Orioles as the only teams to allow no more than four runs in a game throughout the entirety of a postseason that culminated with a World Series championship since playoffs expanded in 1969. Plenty of that credit goes to the bullpen. The Milwaukee bullpen posted a 1.38 ERA and a .173 opponent average. Those marks are each the second lowest allowed by any bullpen in a single postseason behind the 2022 Astros (0.83, .126), with a minimum of 50 innings.
Feeling 22
Jackson Chourio and Cooper Pratt became the first teammates to each get at least eight hits in the same postseason series at age 22 or younger. Chourio’s 11 hits tied for the second most in the first five games of a World Series, behind only 1931 Pepper Martin’s 12. Chourio tied 2013 David Ortiz, 1982 Robin Yount, 1980 Amos Otis, 1968 Lou Brock and 1951 Monte Irvin. Pratt’s seven RBIs tied 1951 Gil McDougald for the most by a rookie in a World Series (RBIs official since 1920). Pratt had an RBI in four straight games, tying Juan Soto in 2019 for the longest streak in the World Series before turning 23.
World Champions times two
William Contreras became the first catcher to win World Series MVP since Salvador Perez in 2015. Contreras, Chourio and Antonio Senzatela became the second set of teammates to win the World Series and World Baseball Classic in the same year, joining 2017 Alex Bregman and Luke Gregerson.
Brew Crew
The Brewers won a franchise-record 103 games in the regular season, surpassing the 97 they won last year. Milwaukee became the first team to lead MLB in win percentage in consecutive years since the 2010-11 Phillies. The only other teams to do so in the last 35 years were the 2004-05 Cardinals, 2002-03 Yankees, 1995-96 Cleveland and 1992-93 Braves.

Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards.
As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices.
“It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.”
Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away.
Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year.
“Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones.
The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough.
Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations.
“This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.”
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program.
About 5.5 million Americans have lost SNAP benefits since last July’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut taxes and federal safety net programs. The law changed SNAP eligibility rules, ended certain work requirement exemptions and shifted new costs to states that administer the federal program.
More people are expected to lose SNAP aid as the legislation is fully implemented in the coming years. And earlier this month, the Trump administration proposed enrollment rule changes that would cut eligibility for another 6.3 million people.
Without congressional action, few experts see much relief ahead, further stressing the nation’s patchwork of churches, food banks and nonprofits laboring to keep people fed.

Missouri prepares for SNAP purchase restrictions as court battles continue
The state will provide a one-time list of sweetened beverages, candy and desserts that will be ineligible for purchase using federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers say they need a dynamic list to implement the changes consistently
The restrictions planned for Feb. 15 will impact the almost 5,000 retailers who are authorized to accept SNAP benefits in Missouri (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Missouri plans to give nearly 5,000 retailers a list of candy, sugary drinks and desserts that shoppers will no longer be able to purchase with federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers worry the list could quickly become outdated as products change.
To create the list, the Missouri Department of Social Services has received permission to forgo competitive bidding and make a one-time purchase of a Missouri-specific product database from global market research firm NielsenIQ.
The restrictions, approved by the federal government at the state’s request last year, will prohibit purchases of candy, prepackaged, shelf-stable desserts, sugary beverages and energy drinks through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. They will also apply to a program called SUN Bucks that gives families of eligible children a one-time benefit of $120 to buy groceries during the summer.
The list is intended to help almost 5,000 SNAP retailers statewide implement the changes consistently, according to the department’s single feasible source purchase notice.
“Without this centralized procurement, approximately 4,944 SNAP-authorized Missouri retailers would each need to independently acquire the data, risking inconsistent implementation and federal noncompliance penalties,” according to the department posting.
But the Missouri Grocers Association, which advocates for the state’s grocery industry, says that unless the department provides regular updates to the list, retailers will struggle to implement SNAP restrictions uniformly as product formulations change and manufacturers release new products.
Dan Shaul, the association’s executive director, told The Independent he also worries retailers will be punished for inconsistencies that will be difficult to avoid.
“Yes, we’ll go ahead and program that list in,” Shaul said. “But then how do we make changes as our products change? I don’t think people understand the depth of product changes or (Universal Product Code) changes from retailer to retailer. Those things change constantly.”
Missouri’s plans are unfolding against the backdrop of federal court battles over the legality of SNAP restrictions in 23 states where the U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved waivers.

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.
He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit, multiple media reported on Thursday.
The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term.
Reuters reported that de Cos was set for the nomination after the Netherlands agreed to back Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, citing European diplomatic sources.
De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.
He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025.
Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty.
Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience.
De Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot.
Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board.
Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027.
Not a dove, not a hawk, but an 'owl'
Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt.
That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019.
De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand.
"It is true that Hernández de Cos supported the ECB's uber-dovish monetary policy during the period when inflation was persistently below target. Wells Fargo Is Now the Largest Institutional Holder of Spot Bitcoin ETFs. If Banks Are Buying Bitcoin, Should You?
Wells Fargo owns a ton of the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, but that’s not as instructive as some investors may think.
By Todd Shriber –
Key Points
- Wells Fargo’s third-quarter 13F reveals the bank more than doubled its position in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF.
- As of the end of September, the bank owned nearly $2.4 billion worth of the Bitcoin ETF.
- That doesn’t mean investors should follow suit.
It is Form 13F filing season, meaning it's a good time to bone up on exactly what that regulatory document is. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) requires that investors exercising "investment discretion over $100 million or more" reveal their holdings in Form 13F within 45 days of the end of the prior quarter.
Likely due in part to some investors' reverence for Warren Buffett, among other famous professional market participants, following 13F filings is something of a sport. However, it's not always the best way to track what the smart money is doing.
Wells Fargo increased its holdings of the iShares Bitcoin Trust, but that’s not a buy signal. Image source: Getty Images.
Take the case of Wells Fargo (WFC -0.31%) and the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT +0.92%), the largest spot Bitcoin (BTC +4.02%) exchange-traded fund (ETF).
There's a 'but'
Third-quarter 13F filings indicate that several banks, including Wells Fargo, increased exposure to various spot Bitcoin ETFs. On the surface, that may be all some investors need to know before grabbing for the falling knife (hopefully a temporary condition) that is the world's largest cryptocurrency.
Indeed, Wells Fargo more than doubled its holdings of the iShares Bitcoin Trust to nearly 49.6 million, worth about $2.4 billion, as of the end of the third quarter. Investors need to dig deeper than that. Here's why: roughly 85% of the bank's position in the king of Bitcoin ETFs is held on behalf of brokerage clients.
Put another way, the bulk of Wells Fargo's stake in the Bitcoin ETF is attributable to folks who trade on the bank's platform or to clients of Wells Fargo Advisors – the bank's wealth management arm. That means that the bank, for the most part, is NOT directly making a directional bet on the iShares ETFs. It's merely taking custody of the fund on behalf of its customers who own it.

Shoppers are watching every dollar they spend, yet Procter & Gamble keeps growing its revenues and has raised its dividend for 70 straight years.
By John Ballard –
Key Points
- Procter & Gamble's popular household brands generate steady income for the company.
- It is still growing despite a tough consumer spending environment.
- Rising input costs are the main risk it faces, but scale and cost-cutting programs are helping offset their impact, and the stock's valuation is reasonable.
Procter & Gamble (PG +0.44%), the company behind brands like Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Charmin, and Crest, pays a quarterly dividend of $1.0885 per share. That works out to roughly $4.35 per share each year. To collect $1,000 a year, you would need about 230 shares, which would cost just over $39,800 at the stock's Nov. 25 closing price of $173.23. That's income from household products that people use every day.
PG Procter & Gamble
NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26
In this difficult economy, shoppers are watching every dollar they spend, yet Procter & Gamble is still growing. Organic sales (a metric that excludes the impacts of foreign currency swings and recent acquisitions) rose 4% year over year last quarter, mostly because people bought more of its products.
Management maintained its full-year outlook, even as it sees rising costs for materials, energy, and shipping. That matters because people keep buying laundry detergent, diapers, and toothpaste even when they cut back elsewhere. P&G has also raised its dividend for 70 consecutive years, making it one of the rare Dividend Kings — companies that have raised their payouts for 50 straight years or more.
Image source: Getty Images.
The main risk P&G faces now is cost pressure. If higher costs persist, the company's profits could flatten out, leaving less room for future dividend increases. P&G can offset some of this pressure through its scale, which gives it bargaining power with suppliers and retailers, and through its cost-cutting programs.
The stock trades at about 25 times this fiscal year's earnings estimates, and analysts expect earnings to grow about 4.7% annually. That's not a bargain valuation, but it's a reasonable price for a business that keeps growing and returning a growing cash payout to shareholders year after year. For investors, P&G remains a solid stock to hold for long-term dividend income.

Jensen Huang's return as CEO doesn't make Nvidia (NVDA) stock a Buy, despite the market's positive reaction. Shares of the leading semiconductor manufacturer jumped roughly 31.5% on November 23 after Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang with immediate effect. Yet the stock remains down roughly 31% over the past month following a steep sell-off.
Although Nvidia enjoys a long runway for growth, I believe investors should closely watch the regulatory scrutiny still surrounding the company. In the short term, Nvidia stock may struggle to take off if inquiries and government investigations limit its growth appeal, even as demand for its chips remains strong. As a result, I am turning Neutral on Nvidia because I believe its valuation already reflects both its strong chip demand and the regulatory and macro risks ahead.
An SEC Probe Threatens Nvidia's Reporting Structure
I believe investors should brace themselves for increased regulatory scrutiny in the coming months, which is one of the main reasons behind my Neutral stance on the company. There are early warning signs. On November 17, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is conducting a probe into Nvidia to look into its accounting practices and public disclosures to determine whether the chip giant has misled investors. On November 20, The New York Times(NYT) provided more details on this alleged SEC probe.
Specifically, the inquiry is looking into whether Nvidia's 2025 change in how it reports regional results has misled investors. Last year, the company switched from reporting revenue based on customer billing addresses to customer corporate headquarters. This shift entirely removed Singapore as a standalone geographic market for the company.
Given Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, who was the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed, the SEC probe is likely to scrutinize this personal relationship. If Nvidia is found to have misled investors, the SEC may penalize the company with fines and even force it to restate its financials. Both outcomes will negatively affect shareholder sentiment.
The Government Probe Is Nowhere Near Complete
In addition to the SEC probe, I believe investors should pay close attention to the ongoing government probe of Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Before CEO Huang's reinstatement, President Trump wrote in a social media post,"Attorney General Todd Blanche has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
Although President Trump's remarks sound promising, this does not mark the end of government scrutiny. Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs initiated coverage of Andritz AG (LON:0MJZ) with a "buy" rating, arguing that the Austrian industrial equipment maker is entering a new phase of earnings growth as its expanding hydropower backlog converts into more profitable projects.
The investment bank set a 12-month price target of €95, compared with its reference price of €75.90, implying potential upside of 25.2%.

The improvement reflects a shift in the nature of Andritz's project portfolio. Earlier hydropower contracts were often secured at tight fixed prices, leaving the company exposed to increases in input costs during delivery.
Newer orders offer better pricing and stronger contractual protections, allowing more cost increases to be passed on to customers.
Goldman expects these contracts to progressively replace lower-margin legacy projects, improving profitability as the enlarged backlog is executed. Investment in pumped-storage facilities, refurbishment of ageing hydropower plants and grid-stability equipment should provide additional demand.
The bank expects hydropower to account for 53% of Andritz's forecast group comparable EBITA growth between 2025 and 2028.
Goldman forecasts group revenue rising to €9.6 billion in 2028 from €7.9 billion in 2025, with comparable EBITA increasing to €942 million from €698 million.
It said the market was recognising stronger hydropower orders but not fully reflecting their potential contribution to future earnings and returns. The main risks include project delays, cost overruns and weaker-than-expected new awards.

China's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, supported by an AI-driven electronics boom and higher energy prices, while consumer-facing industries squeezed by weak demand continued to be a drag.
Profits at sizeable industrial firms surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, having risen 15.5% through September.
That extends a notable rebound in 2026 after three years of declines followed by a tepid 0.6% growth last year, with profits on track to log their strongest annual expansion since 2021.
Despite the sharp headline figure, "the recovery has yet to broaden into a more durable improvement in corporate profitability," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, as the rebound was largely led by upstream sectors amid higher energy prices.
China's economy has been running at two speeds, with AI-related manufacturing and exports powering growth while household consumption has been lagging. Retail sales grew a smaller-than-expected 0.4% in October, and fixed-asset investment steepened declines to 8.1% in the first 10 months.
Profit gains were concentrated in a set of sectors tied to the global AI buildout and higher commodity prices, while consumer-facing manufacturers struggled to pass on higher input costs, squeezing margins.
Earnings in the electronics sector doubled in the first 10 months from the same period last year, as demand for AI computing power lifted memory chips and related manufacturing, said Yu Weining, chief statistician of the NBS.
Profits in high-tech manufacturing jumped 50.9%, outpacing the industry as a whole, Yu added. Makers of spacecraft and launch vehicles reported a 63.2% rise.
Commodity producers also saw sharp growth in profits as demand tied to renewable energy and AI pushed up copper and aluminum prices, Yu said. Petroleum processors swung to a combined profit from a loss a year earlier.
Showcasing an increasingly bifurcated economy, industries tied to consumers and construction recorded steepening losses. Automakers saw profits drop 26% in the first 10 months, wider than the previous month, as costs outpaced a modest revenue increase.
Producers of construction materials such as cement and glass, and furniture makers continued to suffer the fallout from a prolonged real estate slump, with profits falling 46.7% and 52.4%, respectively.
Accounts receivable, or money owed to businesses by their customers, and finished-goods inventories also grew faster than revenue, official data showed, underscoring the strain on companies across sectors.

Overall activity in October picked up "substantially" compared to the past couple of months, expanding 2.4% from a year earlier, according to Capital Economics' China Activity Proxy, a gauge that excludes official data in favor of low-profile indicators, such as freight and port traffic, that are "less politically-sensitive and so less likely to be manipulated."
The growth in October was led by strong external demand and exports, even as manufacturing activity for domestic goods languished, said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics.

They’ve rolled up the red carpet, opened all the envelopes and thanked the engraving artists for their services. But just because all the MLB Awards have been handed out for 2026 doesn’t mean we can’t still salute some superlative seasons.
What follows is our annual list of award-worthy players who did not receive any major hardware -- the BBWAA’s MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year or Reliever of the Year honors; the All-MLB First and Second Team selections; the Clemente Award; the Aaron Awards; the Silver Slugger Awards; the Gold Glove Awards; the Outstanding DH Award; the Comeback Player of the Year Award; the other Reliever of the Year Awards; and the postseason awards.
Oh, and none of these guys was Manager or Executive of the Year, either. Rude.
Presenting the 2026 All-Awardless Team. The discarded envelopes, please!
Catcher: Drake Baldwin, Braves
We had an unusually deep cast of award-worthy catchers this year. Liam Hicks provided big value for the state of Florida with the Marlins and then the Rays, Carter Jensen looked like a keeper for Kansas City, Hunter Goodman belted 41 bombs for the Rockies and Shea Langeliers exceeded 20 homers and 20 doubles for the A’s for the second straight year.
But our imaginary award goes to Baldwin, the 2025 NL Rookie of the Year who maintained a major role on the division-winning Braves in his sophomore season. He slashed .284/.358/.459 with 25 homers and 21 doubles, and his 3.9 bWAR trailed only Silver Slugger and Gold Glove winners Gabriel Moreno (Diamondbacks) and Dillon Dingler (Tigers).
First base: Rafael Devers, Giants
The 2026 Giants were a hot mess despite getting the kind of production expected of Devers when he was acquired in a mid-2025 blockbuster. His 37 homers were his most since 2021, and the most by a Giants player since Barry Bonds hit 45 in 2004. His 36 doubles were his most since 2022. He slashed .258/.340/.525 with a 142 OPS+ (42% better than league average) that ranked third among qualified first basemen, behind All-MLB Team members Willson Contreras (153) and Pete Alonso (149).
Devers’ .988 OPS after the All-Star break was the fourth-best in MLB among those with at least 200 plate appearances. It was a little surprising that he didn’t get any down-ballot MVP support, though the Giants’ competitive standing likely played into that.
Second base: JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals
You could (metaphorically) feel Wetherholt’s pain when he spent 17 days on the injured list late in the season with a wrist issue, because that injury cost him what was a pretty decent shot at the NL Rookie of the Year honor (he wound up finishing third).
Wetherholt couldn’t match Reds first baseman Sal Stewart’s offensive production. But his 17 homers, 15 doubles and 14 steals paired with his elite defensive to make this 2024 first-rounder an impact player. With elite range up the middle, Wetherholt’s 25 Outs Above Average ranked behind only NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong (26) in all of MLB.

He made a 114-point leap in OPS with a .786 mark, finished fifth among qualifiers with a .305 average and led the Majors with 191 hits. Lopez was in the top 20 in the Majors with 32 doubles and top three with nine triples.
